size: Usually 2.5–4 m, big males to 5 m
keys: Huge armoured lizard of rivers and dams
Only the eyes and nostrils show above the water
Basks on sandbanks with the mouth open to cool down

confuse.how: Monitor is far slimmer, with a long thin neck and forked tongue, and runs off fast

behaviour: Ambushes animals that come to drink, from fish and birds to impala and wildebeest, and drags them under. Females bury eggs in sand and guard the nest, then carry the hatchlings to the water in their mouth.
bite: Attacks come at the water's edge: keep several metres from the bank of any dam or river and never wade or fetch water where crocodiles can live.
memo: Stay away from the edge.

keys: Big lizard with a long neck and long flattened tail
Dark olive with rows of yellow spots and bands
Forked tongue flicking in and out
Always near water, swims well

confuse.how: Rock monitor is greyer and stockier, with a rounded tail, away from water
Crocodile is bulkier, armoured, with a huge head

behaviour: Eats crabs, frogs, fish, birds and their eggs, and digs up crocodile nests. Lays its eggs inside termite mounds, where the termites seal them in.
bite: Not venomous but bites hard and lashes with the tail when caught.
memo: The yellow-spotted lizard of the water.

keys: Stocky grey-brown monitor with pale blotches
Bulbous snout, rounded tail
Far from water, often in trees or burrows

confuse.how: Slimmer, darker, with yellow spots and a flattened tail, near water

behaviour: Wanders widely in search of snails, millipedes, beetles, eggs and small animals, even venomous snakes. Hides in burrows and tree holes.
bite: Not venomous; a big one bites hard and holds on.
memo: The monitor of the dry bush.

keys: High-domed shell, yellow with black spots and flecks
The largest tortoise here
Often crossing roads after rain

confuse.how: Smaller, flatter shell with a hinge at the back

behaviour: Grazes grasses and succulents, gnaws old bones and hyena droppings for calcium. Lives for decades.
memo: Help it across the road in the direction it was going.

keys: Flattish brown shell with darker, pale-centred plates
A hinge across the back of the shell closes over the hind legs

confuse.how: Much bigger, high-domed, no hinge

behaviour: Eats mushrooms, millipedes, snails and plants; hides in rock cracks and under logs in the dry season.
memo: A tortoise that shuts its back door.

keys: Big terrapin with a serrated back edge to the shell
Hinged plastron at the front closes over the head
Basks on rocks and logs in rivers and dams

confuse.how: Smaller, flatter, no hinge, in pans that dry out

behaviour: Eats snails, insects, fish, fruit and carrion. Slides off its basking log at the first sign of danger.
memo: The big terrapin of the dams, with a jagged shell.

keys: Flat olive-brown shell, no hinge
Head drawn in sideways
Appears in rain pools and walks overland between pans

confuse.how: Bigger, serrated shell edge, in permanent water

behaviour: Buries itself in the mud when the pan dries and waits for the rains. Picks ticks off warthogs and rhinos wallowing in the water, and can gang up to pull doves under as they drink.
memo: The terrapin of the rain pools.

keys: Green to yellow-brown, changes colour
Flaps of skin at the back of the head
Eyes that move separately; feet like tongs
Turns pale and easy to spot by torchlight at night
behaviour: Catches insects with a tongue longer than its body. When threatened it inflates, opens the flaps, gapes an orange mouth and hisses. Boomslangs and birds are its main enemies.
bite: Not venomous; it can nip when handled.
memo: Look for a pale shape on a branch at night.

keys: Big lizard on tree trunks, black patch on the side of the neck
Breeding males have a bright blue head and throat
Head-bobs at rivals

confuse.how: Lives on the ground, smaller, spiny

behaviour: Watches from a trunk head-down and drops to catch ants, beetles and termites. Hides on the far side of the trunk when you approach.
bite: Harmless, though it gapes and bites if caught.
memo: The blue-headed lizard of the tree trunk.

keys: Spiny grey-brown lizard of open sandy ground
Broad head; breeding males with blue cheeks
Rests in the shade of a bush, near its burrow

confuse.how: Bigger, on tree trunks, black neck patch

behaviour: Eats mostly ants.
memo: The spiny lizard of the bare ground.

keys: Young and females black with three cream stripes and a bright blue tail
Adult males bronze-brown with pale speckles
On granite rocks and outcrops, in groups

confuse.how: Brown with two pale stripes, no blue tail, on trees and buildings

behaviour: Basks on rocks and chases insects; the blue tail draws an attack away from the body and breaks off.
memo: Blue tails on the granite.

keys: Glossy brown skink with two pale stripes along the back
Smooth shiny scales
Common on tree trunks, rocks and camp walls

confuse.how: Smaller, with a white stripe along each side, usually on the ground

behaviour: Basks on trunks and walls and catches insects, often around lights in camp.
memo: The skink on the camp wall.

keys: Brown with a white stripe along each side, below a dark band
Small, quick, in leaf litter and grass

confuse.how: Bigger, stripes on the back, climbs

behaviour: Hunts small insects on the ground under bushes.
memo: A side-striped ground skink.

keys: Smooth shiny brown skink with tiny legs
Wriggles like a snake when uncovered
Under logs and stones, in sand

confuse.how: No legs at all, bigger and dark grey

behaviour: Swims through loose soil hunting termites and larvae.
memo: A skink that swims in the sand.

keys: No legs: looks like a smooth dark grey snake
Blunt head and blunt tail, tiny eyes
Found by digging or after rain

confuse.how: A real snake has a forked tongue and belly scales in a single row

behaviour: Burrows in moist soil and leaf litter and eats earthworms and larvae; gives birth to live young.
memo: A lizard that lost its legs.

keys: Tiny bronze skink with a pale stripe on the side
Eyes covered by a transparent fixed lid, like a snake
In leaf litter

confuse.how: Bigger, with a dark band above the white side stripe

behaviour: Darts through dry leaves hunting tiny insects.
memo: The smallest skink, snake-eyed.

keys: Tiny grey-brown gecko with a dark line through the eye
Active by day, unlike most geckos
Round pupils

confuse.how: Bigger, pale, comes out at night around lights

behaviour: Runs about tree trunks and walls by day catching tiny insects; often on fence posts.
memo: The tiny gecko of the daytime.

keys: Big stocky gecko covered in raised tubercles
Grey-brown with dark crossbars
Clicks loudly at night

confuse.how: Slimmer, paler, smoother skin

behaviour: Hunts beetles, moths and other geckos on rocks and trees at night.
memo: The big warty gecko that clicks.

keys: Pale, almost see-through grey gecko with faint dark bands
Wide toe pads, walks on ceilings
Gathers around lights at night

confuse.how: Bigger and much wartier

behaviour: Waits by lamps for the insects they draw; chirps to its neighbours.
memo: The gecko on the ceiling.

keys: Large gecko with soft, velvety skin
Grey with dark wavy bands
Hides under bark and in hollow trees

confuse.how: Warty, not velvety skin

behaviour: Hunts insects on trunks at night.
memo: The velvet gecko.

keys: Small ground gecko with a pointed snout
Fine speckles of pale spots
Under stones and in old termite mounds

confuse.how: Climbs and is active by day

behaviour: Hunts termites and other small insects at night.
memo: The speckled gecko of the ground.

keys: Very flat gecko that slides into narrow rock cracks
Grey-brown with dark crossbands
On granite outcrops

confuse.how: Thicker, warty, not flattened

behaviour: Lives in groups in rock cracks and hunts on the rock faces at night.
memo: A gecko flattened to fit the cracks.

keys: Very big, heavy lizard of rocky outcrops
Dark brown with pale spots; breeding males with a pink-purple head
Plated, stiff-looking body with a fold along the side

confuse.how: Monitor has a long neck, forked tongue and loose skin

behaviour: Eats insects, flowers, fruit and smaller lizards; wedges itself into a crack when disturbed.
memo: The giant of the koppies.

keys: Slender brown lizard with a long tail
A yellow-edged black stripe along each side
Yellow throat (red in breeding males)

confuse.how: Stockier, uniform brown with rough scales

behaviour: Moves fast through grass and bush hunting insects; dives into a burrow.
memo: Yellow lines along a slender lizard.

keys: Stocky, uniform brown lizard with rough plate-like scales
Fold of skin along the side
Lives in termite mounds and rock piles

confuse.how: Darker, spotted, on rock faces

behaviour: Eats insects, fruit and flowers; grunts and hisses when caught.
memo: A brick-brown lizard of the termite mounds.

keys: Adults sandy with pale stripes and dark bars
Young are black with white markings and walk stiff-legged
The young imitate the oogpister beetle, which squirts acid
behaviour: Darts between bushes on sandy ground hunting termites. The jerky black-and-white young fool predators into taking them for a beetle that sprays acid.
memo: A baby lizard dressed as a stinking beetle.

keys: Very flat lizard on rock faces
Males brilliantly coloured: green head, blue body, orange-red tail
Females and young dark with three pale stripes

confuse.how: Not flat; females have a blue tail

behaviour: Lives in colonies on granite, catching flies and eating figs that fall on the rock.
memo: The flat rainbow of the rocks.

keys: Small spiny lizard with rings of spiky scales on the tail
Brown with darker blotches
Hides in holes and cracks of tree trunks

confuse.how: Bigger, smooth tail, blue head in males

behaviour: Wedges itself into a crack with its spiny tail blocking the entrance.
memo: A spiky tail that plugs the hole.

keys: Big dark scorpion with slender pincers and a very thick tail
Can squirt venom up to a metre
Hides under stones and logs, in sandy ground

confuse.how: Burrowing scorpion has huge pincers and a thin tail: much less dangerous

behaviour: The most dangerous scorpion in South Africa. Hunts insects and spiders at night. Raises the tail and rasps it when threatened, and can spray venom at the eyes.
bite: Intense burning pain, then tingling, muscle twitching, sweating, difficulty swallowing and breathing; children and the elderly are most at risk. Keep calm and still, hospital: a scorpion antivenom exists. Venom in the eyes: rinse with lots of water.
memo: Thin pincers and a thick tail: dangerous.

keys: Yellow-brown thick-tailed scorpion with slender pincers
Tail thick and rough, darker at the end

confuse.how: Bigger and darker, even more venomous

behaviour: Hides in shallow scrapes under stones and comes out on warm nights.
bite: Severe pain and sometimes neurotoxic signs; children at risk. Hospital.
memo: Treat every thick-tailed scorpion as dangerous.

keys: Small olive-brown scorpion with slender pincers and tail
Often under bark and in houses

confuse.how: Much bigger, with a very thick tail

behaviour: Climbs well, hiding under loose bark by day.
bite: A painful sting like a bee's, no lasting effect.
memo: A small bark scorpion: painful, not dangerous.

keys: Big shiny scorpion with large, heavy pincers
Thin tail
Digs deep burrows, often at the base of a stone

confuse.how: Slender pincers and a very thick tail: dangerous

behaviour: Waits at the burrow mouth at night and crushes insects in its pincers rather than stinging.
bite: Pinches hard; the sting is mild.
memo: Big pincers, thin tail: mostly harmless.

size: 15–20 cm, males with very long tails
keys: Very flat, dark scorpion of rock cracks
Big flat pincers, thin tail; the longest scorpion in the world
Lives in granite crevices

confuse.how: Not flattened, lives in a burrow

behaviour: Wedges itself into narrow cracks and catches insects passing at the entrance. Gentle, rarely stings.
bite: Mild.
memo: The flat giant of the rock cracks.

keys: Flattened dark scorpion under tree bark
Strong pincers, thin tail

confuse.how: Paler and more slender

behaviour: Lives under the loose bark of dead trees.
bite: Mild.
memo: The scorpion under the bark.

keys: Huge golden-yellow web strung between trees, often across paths
Big female with banded legs (black and yellow)
Tiny males wait at the edge of the web

confuse.how: Has tufts of hair on the legs

behaviour: The golden silk is so strong that small birds get caught. Webs are rebuilt piece by piece, often in groups along a game path.
bite: Harmless.
memo: Golden webs across the path in summer.

keys: Golden orb-web spider with black hairy tufts on the legs
Silvery-white body with spots

confuse.how: Banded legs without tufts

behaviour: Strings golden webs in more shaded, wooded places.
bite: Harmless.
memo: Golden web, hairy knees.

keys: Body banded yellow, black and silver
Sits head-down in the centre of the web, legs in pairs forming an X
Zigzag bands of white silk in the web

confuse.how: Golden web, long body, higher up

behaviour: Builds in grass and low bushes; shakes the web hard when disturbed.
bite: Harmless.
memo: An X in the grass.

keys: Small spider with a hard, flat body bearing six spines
Bright colours: red, yellow, white and black
Sits in a round web between branches
behaviour: The hard spiny body puts off birds.
bite: Harmless.
memo: A spiny jewel in the web.

keys: Big hairy brown tarantula
A soft horn sticking backward from the top of the body
Lives in a silk-lined burrow

confuse.how: Golden-brown, no horn

behaviour: Waits at its burrow mouth at night for beetles and crickets. Rears up showing its fangs when bothered.
bite: Painful bite, mild venom; the hairs irritate.
memo: A baboon spider with a horn.

keys: Large golden-brown hairy tarantula
Thick legs with dark bands at the joints
Burrow with a silk collar

confuse.how: Has a horn on its back

behaviour: Ambushes at the burrow at night; males roam after the first rains looking for females.
bite: Painful, not dangerous.
memo: The golden baboon spider.

keys: Round shiny black body, sometimes with a red stripe or spots on top
Small; long thin black legs
Messy web low down, with a round egg sac

confuse.how: Brown, with an orange hourglass below and spiky egg sacs

behaviour: Builds low in grass, stones and old burrows; bites only when pressed against skin.
bite: Painful cramps spreading from the bite to the belly and chest, sweating, rising blood pressure, after 30–60 minutes. Hospital: an antivenom exists and works.
memo: A black button: the dangerous one.

keys: Round brown body with a geometric pattern
Orange hourglass under the belly
Spiky, round egg sacs like little mines

confuse.how: Black and shiny, smooth egg sacs

behaviour: Very common under furniture, in corners of buildings and in tree holes.
bite: Local pain, rarely more.
memo: Spiky egg sacs: the brown one, mild.

keys: Pale brown spider with long legs
Darker violin-shaped mark on the front of the body
Six eyes in pairs; runs fast

confuse.how: Yellowish, with no violin mark

behaviour: Hunts at night and hides in clothes, shoes and bedding by day.
bite: Often not felt at first; a slow-healing ulcer can develop over days. See a doctor.
memo: Shake out shoes and clothes.

keys: Pale yellow to cream spider with darker jaws
Long front legs
Hides by day in a small silk sac in a fold of curtain or leaf

confuse.how: Brown, with a violin mark

behaviour: Wanders indoors at night and bites when trapped against skin, often in bed.
bite: A blister, then a slow-healing sore; most people heal with no treatment, but see a doctor if it spreads.
memo: The pale spider in the curtains.

keys: Huge, fast huntsman spider, brown and flattened
Black and orange bands under the legs
Comes into houses before rain
behaviour: Hunts insects and geckos; the female guards a large ball-shaped egg nest of silk and leaves.
bite: Painful but harmless.
memo: Big and scary, harmless: leave it to eat the mosquitoes.

keys: Big grey nests of silk and debris in thorn trees
Hundreds of small velvety spiders share each nest
Sheets of web around the nest catch insects
behaviour: Lives in colonies that hunt together and share their prey; the young are fed by the females, which die and are eaten by them.
bite: Harmless.
memo: The grey balls of web in the thorn trees.

keys: Very flat, with spiny grasping front arms
Extremely long, whip-like first pair of legs used as feelers
Moves sideways like a crab
behaviour: Not a spider: no venom, no silk. Hunts insects on rock faces and walls at night.
bite: Harmless.
memo: Scary looks, no venom at all.

keys: Large tick with long mouthparts
Back with green-gold and orange enamel-like patterns
Legs banded
behaviour: Waits on grass and runs towards the carbon dioxide of breath. Feeds on buffalo, rhino, giraffe and people. Passes on the bacteria of tick-bite fever.
bite: Tick-bite fever: headache, fever and a black scab at the bite, 5–7 days later. Tell a doctor you were in the bush: it is treated with antibiotics. Check your body every evening and remove ticks with tweezers, close to the skin.
memo: Check yourself every evening.

keys: Grey to whitish tree frog, turns almost white in the sun
Big sticky toe pads, long legs
Its white foam nests hang from branches over water
voice: Soft croaks and squeaks on rainy summer nights.

confuse.how: Brown, with a darker back patch and big bulging eyes, lives on the ground

behaviour: Several males and a female beat a foam nest the size of a fist over a pan; the tadpoles drop into the water a few days later. Spends the dry season in walls and roofs, often in camp.
memo: The white frog of the foam nests.

keys: Small reed frog, boldly painted: stripes or spots of black, yellow, white and red
Red-pink feet
Clings to reeds over water
voice: Short, piercing whistles in chorus, painful up close.
behaviour: Gathers in big choruses in reeds round pans and dams after the rains.
memo: A painted jewel in the reeds.

keys: Brown tree frog with big bulging eyes
Dark horseshoe-shaped patch on the back
Vertical pupil
voice: A short 'yack' followed by a buzz, from bushes.

confuse.how: Grey to white, no back patch

behaviour: Calls from low bushes; lays its eggs in a burrow near water and the tadpoles wriggle to the pool.
memo: Big eyes and a horseshoe.

keys: Olive with three dark stripes down the back
Walks or runs rather than hops
voice: A loud liquid 'quoip', like a bubble popping: one of the sounds of a rainy night.
behaviour: Calls hidden in grass at the edge of pans.
memo: The bubble-popping frog.

keys: Shiny black with two red bands down the sides
Rubbery skin, walks
Bright colours warn that its skin is toxic
behaviour: Spends the dry season in termite mounds and under rocks; its skin secretes toxins that can kill other frogs kept with it.
bite: The skin secretion irritates eyes and cuts: wash your hands after touching it.
memo: Red and black: don't lick.

keys: Big, stout olive frog with a broad head
Pale stripe down the middle of the back
Appears in numbers after the first heavy rains
voice: A deep 'whoop', like a cow lowing in the distance.

confuse.how: Warty, dry skin, crawls

behaviour: Spends the dry months buried in a cocoon, comes out to breed in pans for a few days. Males guard the tadpoles and dig channels to save them when the water drops.
bite: Bites hard if handled.
memo: The frog that guards its tadpoles.

keys: Red-brown toad, smooth for a toad
Two dark spots on the lower back
No obvious bulge behind the eyes
voice: A long, deep 'whoo' repeated, from deep water.

confuse.how: Wartier, with a red patch on the thighs and a cross on the head

behaviour: Often in houses and bathrooms. Tadpoles gather in great swirling schools.
memo: The red toad in the bathroom.

keys: Large warty toad, brown with dark blotches
Pale cross on top of the head
Red patches on the back of the thighs

confuse.how: No cross on the head, more uniform olive

behaviour: Hunts insects under the camp lights. The glands behind the eyes produce a toxin that makes dogs sick.
memo: A cross on the head, a snore at night.

keys: Big olive to yellow-brown toad with paired dark blotches
Large glands behind the eyes
No cross on the head

confuse.how: Pale cross on the head, red on the thighs

behaviour: Breeds in pans after rain; spends the day buried.
memo: The big olive toad of the bushveld.

keys: Tiny flat toad, grey-brown with darker blotches
Lives on granite outcrops
behaviour: Breeds in rock pools after rain.
memo: A thumbnail toad of the rocks.

keys: Round, almost ball-shaped frog with a short face
Brown with paler and darker blotches
Tiny legs: it walks and digs backwards
voice: A short chirp repeated, from the ground on warm wet nights.

confuse.how: Pointed, shovel-shaped snout, digs head first

behaviour: Lives underground and comes up after rain. The eggs develop straight into froglets in a burrow, with no tadpole. Puffs up when threatened.
memo: A grumpy ball that digs backwards.

keys: Pointed, hard shovel-like snout
Tiny eyes, smooth mottled skin
Digs head first
voice: A long insect-like buzz from the ground near pans.

confuse.how: Round, short-faced, digs backwards

behaviour: The female guards her eggs in a burrow, then digs a tunnel to lead the tadpoles to the water.
memo: A frog with a spade on its nose.

keys: Slim, pointed frog with ridges along the back
Very long legs, huge jumps
Red-brown, often with a pale back stripe
voice: A short, high trill like a ricocheting bullet.

confuse.how: Bigger, smoother, near permanent water

behaviour: Leaps several metres when disturbed, zigzagging off.
memo: The champion jumper.

keys: Big green to brown frog of rivers and dams
Long pointed snout, smooth skin
Long webbed hind feet
voice: A rattling series of clucks ending in a croak.

confuse.how: Smaller, ridged back, in pans

behaviour: Sits at the edge of permanent water and leaps in when approached.
memo: The frog of the river bank.

keys: Small, warty brown frog of puddles
Often a pale line down the back
Floats among the grass at the edge
behaviour: Calls by day and night from shallow flooded grass.
memo: The little snorer of the puddles.

keys: Squat, marbled grey-brown frog
Hard spade on the hind feet for digging
On sandy river banks
voice: A fast, high piping 'tic-tic-tic', like a hammer on metal.

confuse.how: Round with a tiny face, no long legs

behaviour: Buries itself in sand by day.
memo: The sand digger that taps like a hammer.

keys: Flat, slimy frog that never leaves the water
Black claws on the inner toes of the hind feet
Eyes on top of the head, no tongue
behaviour: Feeds on anything it can push into its mouth with its hands; walks overland between pans on rainy nights.
memo: A frog with claws and no tongue.

keys: Big black-and-copper dung beetle
Rolls dung balls bigger than itself
Active in the heat of the day in summer
behaviour: Shapes a ball from fresh dung of elephant or rhino, rolls it away backwards and buries it with an egg inside. Dung beetles clear tonnes of dung, feed the soil and kill fly larvae.
memo: Don't drive over them on the road after rain.

keys: Shining metallic green beetle with orange-brown legs
Males with a forked horn on the head
Fast, buzzing flight
behaviour: Feeds on sap oozing from wounded trees and on ripe fruit.
memo: A green jewel on the sap.

keys: Big, black, slow beetle with a hard ridged shell
Cannot fly: wing covers fused
Walks along roads and paths

confuse.how: Faster, with white spots and an acid spray

behaviour: A tok-tokkie relative: scavenges dead plant matter and dung.
memo: A black tank on the road.

keys: Large black ground beetle with white side patches on the thorax
Long legs, runs very fast
Raises its rear when threatened

confuse.how: Slow, no white marks, harmless

behaviour: A fierce hunter of other insects. Its name means 'eye-squirter': it sprays formic acid at the face.
bite: Acid in the eyes stings badly: rinse with lots of water.
memo: Eye-squirter: look, don't pick up.

keys: Black with bands of yellow-orange spots on the wing covers
Slow flight from flower to flower
Named for its colours, like the old Cape Mounted Rifles
behaviour: Eats flowers, especially of beans and pumpkins. Its larvae eat grasshopper eggs.
bite: Crushing it on the skin releases cantharidin: painful blisters.
memo: Black and yellow bands: don't squash it on your skin.

keys: Huge brown longhorn beetle
Long antennae, strong jaws
Comes to lights at night in summer
behaviour: Larvae tunnel for years in dead wood.
bite: Can nip hard with its jaws.
memo: The giant at the lamp.

keys: Ladybird with an orange-red pattern of crescents on black
Round, shiny
behaviour: Eats aphids, larvae and adults alike.
memo: A ladybird with moons.

keys: Builds the tall hard termite mounds of the bushveld
Workers pale, soldiers with big brown heads
Winged swarms come out after the first rains

confuse.how: No mound: small dark workers cut grass by day

behaviour: Farms a fungus on chewed plant matter inside the mound. Mounds are the richest patches of the bush: trees grow on them, aardvarks dig them, mongooses, monitors and snakes live in them, and the swarming alates feed everything from birds to people.
bite: Soldiers bite and draw blood.
memo: The architects of the bush.

keys: Dark brown termites working in the open, on cool days
Cut grass into short lengths and carry them underground
Small heaps of soil around holes, no mound

confuse.how: Pale, builds tall mounds, never seen in the open

behaviour: Compete with grazers for grass, and are eaten by aardwolves and bat-eared foxes.
memo: Termites that mow the grass.

keys: Large black ants marching in a column
They squeak when disturbed
Return carrying termites in their jaws

confuse.how: Brown and black, runs everywhere rather than in columns

behaviour: Raids termite galleries in columns of hundreds. Wounded ants are carried home and treated by their nest-mates.
bite: A very painful sting.
memo: Black columns that raid termites.

keys: Fast, aggressive ants, black with a reddish-brown thorax
Swarm and bite when their nest is touched
Nest entrances in sandy ground

confuse.how: All black, bigger, marching in columns

behaviour: Tend aphids and scale insects for honeydew and attack anything near the nest.
bite: Many small painful bites.
memo: Don't stand on their nest.

keys: Brown and black banded bee
Wild colonies in hollow trees, rock cracks and roofs
African bees defend their nest fiercely

confuse.how: Big, black and hairy, solitary

behaviour: The bushveld's main pollinator, followed by honeyguides and honey badgers to their nests. Elephants avoid them: farmers use hives as fences.
bite: Scrape the sting out. Many stings, or swelling of the face and breathing trouble (allergy), need hospital at once. Walk away from a disturbed nest fast, towards shelter.
memo: Leave the nest alone.

keys: Big, black, hairy bee with yellow-white bands
Loud buzz
Bores nest holes in dead wood and thatch

confuse.how: Smaller, brown, lives in colonies

behaviour: Pollinates large flowers; robs nectar by biting through the base of others.
bite: Rarely stings.
memo: The bumblebee of the bush.

keys: Looks like a big hairy ant, black with red or white spots
Females wingless, run on the ground
Squeaks when held

confuse.how: No spots, in columns

behaviour: A wasp, not an ant: the female lays her eggs on bee and wasp larvae.
bite: An extremely painful sting.
memo: A wasp in ant's clothing.

keys: Orange-brown with a black wingtip crossed by white spots
Slow, floating flight
Black-and-white spotted body

confuse.how: Smaller, more transparent wings with black dots

behaviour: Caterpillars eat milkweeds and store their poisons: birds avoid the adults, and other butterflies copy its colours.
memo: The model all the others copy.

keys: Large black butterfly with yellow bands and spots
Red and blue eyespots near the hindwing
Fast, gliding flight
behaviour: Caterpillars, which look like bird droppings when young, eat citrus and wild relatives.
memo: The big yellow-and-black swallowtail.

keys: Black wings with a bright blue spot on each hindwing
White spots at the wingtips
Basks with wings flat on bare ground
behaviour: Males defend a patch of bare ground and chase off anything that passes.
memo: Black with a blue eye.

keys: White butterfly with dark veins and a dark border
Huge migrations heading north-east in summer

confuse.how: Plain white to green-yellow, no dark veins

behaviour: Some summers millions fly over the lowveld in the same direction for days. Caterpillars eat shepherd's tree and other capers.
memo: The white flood of summer.

keys: Grey wings covered in black-edged white dots, like a guineafowl
Settles on paths with wings spread
behaviour: Feeds on fermenting fruit and dung; caterpillars eat bushwillows.
memo: A guineafowl's feather that flies.

keys: Plain white (males) or greenish-yellow (females) butterfly
Fast, direct flight
Often migrating in numbers

confuse.how: Dark veins and wing border

behaviour: Caterpillars feed on cassia relatives.
memo: A plain white in a hurry.

keys: Small orange-brown butterfly with thin, almost see-through wings
Black dots and a dark wing border
Weak, fluttering flight

confuse.how: Bigger, black wingtip with white spots

behaviour: Acraeas are distasteful to birds, and fly slowly as if they knew it.
memo: The slow little orange dancer.

keys: Tiny blue butterfly
Underside with zebra-like brown and white bands
Thin tails on the hindwings
behaviour: The tail and eyespots fool birds into pecking the wrong end.
memo: A tiny blue with zebra stripes beneath.

keys: White butterfly with a bright scarlet tip on the forewing
Black border to the tip

confuse.how: No coloured tip

behaviour: Caterpillars eat shepherd's tree and other caper bushes.
memo: Scarlet tips.

keys: Big, powerful orange and black butterfly
Two tails on each hindwing
Fast, strong flight round the treetops
behaviour: Drinks fermenting fruit, sap and dung rather than nectar.
memo: The tailed emperor on rotten fruit.

keys: Caterpillar black, red and white with spiky tufts, on mopane
Moth brown-orange with a big eyespot on each hindwing
behaviour: Caterpillars appear in huge numbers in summer and can strip mopane trees bare.
memo: Mopane worms: a delicacy, millions are harvested.

keys: Huge pale green moth with long trailing tails
Eyespots on all four wings
behaviour: Adults have no mouth and live a few days. Caterpillars eat marula. The tails confuse the sonar of bats.
memo: A green kite at the lamp.

keys: Brown papery silk nests in trees
Hairy caterpillars that march nose to tail in long lines

confuse.how: Spider nests are grey, messy, full of debris

behaviour: Caterpillars live together in the silk bag and leave in processions to feed.
bite: Their hairs cause an itchy rash and eye irritation.
memo: Hairy queues: don't touch.

keys: Grey-brown moth that flies in at dusk
Comes to beer, wine and fruit
Wing pattern of wavy lines
behaviour: Drinks fermenting fruit juice; caterpillars eat acacias.
memo: The moth that comes for a sundowner.

keys: Males bright red with red veins in the wings
Perches on stems at the water's edge
Wings held forward and down

confuse.how: Broader, flatter red body, no red wing veins

behaviour: Males hold small territories at the water's edge and chase off rivals.
memo: Red veins in the wings.

keys: Males scarlet with a broad, flat body
Wings clear with an amber patch at the base

confuse.how: Thinner body, red veins

behaviour: One of the first dragonflies at new pans after rain.
memo: The flat scarlet.

keys: Golden-yellow dragonfly, always on the wing
Swarms over open ground before storms
behaviour: The world's greatest insect traveller: generations cross the Indian Ocean on the monsoon winds.
memo: The golden glider of the storm.

keys: Big black-and-yellow dragonfly
Club-shaped tip to the tail
Perches on sticks over dams
behaviour: Hunts other dragonflies from a lookout perch.
memo: A tiger-striped club.

keys: Damselfly of streams and rivers
Males with white and red legs flattened like paddles
Blue body
behaviour: Males dance in front of females, waving their bright legs.
memo: Dancing legs over the stream.

keys: Bright green, black, yellow and orange grasshopper
Short wings, crawls more than it flies
Gathers in groups

confuse.how: Bigger, with warty red spots and a foul foam

behaviour: Feeds on poisonous plants and is distasteful to birds, hence its colours.
memo: A painted grasshopper: don't eat.

keys: Big grasshopper with a warty thorax spotted red
Wings with red and blue flashes
Squirts a bitter foam when handled

confuse.how: Smaller, smooth, short-winged

behaviour: Eats milkweeds and stores their poison.
bite: The foam irritates; wash your hands.
memo: Warts and foam.

keys: Fat, spiny, flightless cricket
Squirts yellow blood from its joints when handled
Crawls along roads
behaviour: Eats anything, including others of its kind run over on the road.
bite: Bites hard.
memo: A spiny tank that bleeds on you.

keys: Large green praying mantis
A pale spot on each forewing
Grasping front legs held folded

confuse.how: Brown, thin as a twig

behaviour: Waits motionless for flies, bees and moths; often at camp lights.
memo: The green mantis at the lamp.

keys: Thin grey-brown mantis that looks exactly like a twig
Sways in the wind when it moves

confuse.how: Green and broad

behaviour: Hunts on bare branches where its camouflage is perfect.
memo: A twig that hunts.

keys: Stout insect with clear or mottled wings, on tree trunks
Hard to see, easy to hear: the loud summer buzz of the bush
behaviour: Nymphs live underground for years sucking root sap; adults sing on the trunks in the heat.
memo: The sound of a hot summer day.

keys: Shiny black bug with a red-orange cross on the back
Young are red, gathered in groups
behaviour: Hunts millipedes in groups, injecting saliva that liquefies them.
bite: Painful if handled.
memo: The cross-backed millipede killer.

keys: Small brown mosquito that bites at night
Rests and bites with its body tilted up at an angle
Breeds in small sunny pools after rain
behaviour: Only the females bite, from dusk to dawn. The lowveld is a malaria area, with most cases in the wet season.
bite: Long sleeves at dusk, repellent and nets. A fever, headache or flu-like illness up to a few months after a visit: see a doctor and say where you were, malaria can be treated if caught early.
memo: Dusk: sleeves and repellent.
